newsitem.title: GERMANY: German press strains to explain Kohl's record run.
newsitem.headline: German press strains to explain Kohl's record run.

text.p: The German media, straining to explain how Helmut Kohl has stayed in power for a record 14 years, has begun comparing the veteran chancellor to TV series stars, tranquillisers and familiar old rubber plants.

Television talk shows looking ahead to October 30, when he breaks Konrad Adenauer's record as the longest-serving postwar chancellor, are sounding more like political science parodies as they dig ever deeper for the secret of Kohl's success.

The problem for the press is that Kohl, 66, has been around so long that he, as one journalist remarked in a talk round on Sunday, "is like a rubber plant, we think he's old-fashioned and we don't like him, but we've gotten so used to him."

"There is nothing new to report about the man," Joerg Hafkemeyer, a correspondent for WDR television in Cologne, complained on the same "Press Club" show on ARD TV. "Go ahead, just try to find out something new about him..."
That has not stopped journalists from trying to explain how Kohl, who for years was looked down on as a provincial oaf, now ranks as the towering statesman of Europe.

"Chancellor Kohl is the unspectacular star in a TV series," Hafkemeyer ventured by way of explanation. While his series just runs and runs, the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) keep changing their plots and swapping out their leading men.
"And just look where their ratings are -- in the basement."
Horst-Eberhard Richter, one of Germany's best-known popular psychologists, presented his favourite theory in the SAT 1 "Talk in the Tower" discussion round on Sunday evening.
"I always say Kohl is something like a mild sedative," the white-haired professor explained. "He calms things down and puts conflicts to rest."
Kohl, the only chancellor many young Germans have ever known, also plays the role of father figure to voters upset by the rapid changes of recent years, Richter added.
"We have a younger generation that is convinced things are going to get worse in the next few decades," he said. "They are ready to seek a fatherly person to reassure them."
According to Rudolf Scharping, the SPD's failed challenger to Kohl in the 1994 election, the media's current fascination with Kohl is just a reaction to its earlier rejection.
"There was just about unbounded criticism of Kohl in the beginning and I suspect this has now turned into equally unbounded genuflecting before him," he said on SAT 1.

Karl Feldmeyer of the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said Kohl's secret was that he was the only politician in Bonn who wanted power for a goal -- European integration -- rather than simply for its own sake.
"Europe is his life's work," he said, "and if this failed, I'm sure we would then know when the Kohl era will end."

"Being chancellor is only a side job -- his real job is European Union foreign minister," Hafkemeyer added. "He could actually govern any European country. From Spain to Moscow, they go bananas when he comes for a visit."
Even Der Spiegel, the liberal newsweekly that gleefully ran headlines like "Kohl kaputt" for years, has finally capitulated before the chancellor's record run.
A recent Spiegel cover story bestowed on him the title of "eternal chancellor" and said Germany was a "Kohlocracy."
